What we look at before we price the work

On a 1961 house the wall area outside is usually small and the detail is not. Fascia, soffit, the garage door surround, the front entry and the window trim is a narrow band of work that adds up, and it is exactly what gets underestimated by anyone quoting off photographs instead of standing there. 47.6 percent of the housing sits in buildings of two units or more, which means hallways, stairwells and unit turnarounds are as much of the work as living rooms. Those get quoted per unit and they get done to a date.

What should be on a written quote in Blue Island

  • Containment, not just paint. 71.9 percent of housing in Blue Island was built before 1980, so on most addresses here the lead-safe setup and the cleanup are part of the job and part of the hours.
  • Plaster as well as drywall. 26.7 percent of Blue Island is prewar. Plaster cracks along the lath and comes back if it is only filled, so wall repair is a different line from wall painting.
  • Setup does not shrink with the room. The median unit here is 5.1 rooms. Masking, cutting in and cleanup cost the same in a small room as a large one, so a flat per-room rate is usually wrong in one direction or the other.
  • Per unit, to a date. 47.6 percent of units here are in buildings of two or more. Turnover work is priced per unit and scheduled to a move-out, not to the weather.

What the housing here is likely made of

Most of it is 1960s brick and brick-and-frame, with a large share of it in buildings of two units or more. Association and landlord work is as much of the Blue Island market as single-house work.

Two figures produce that sentence and no others: build year 1961, and a stock that is 44.1 percent detached, 3.8 percent attached and 47.6 percent in buildings of two or more.

Read it as a starting assumption rather than a finding. No public dataset records what the walls in Blue Island are made from, so attaching a number to it would mean inventing one. The house itself answers faster than any table can.

What the age of Blue Island houses means for lead paint

The honest answer for a 1960s-era house in Blue Island is probably yes, there is older paint under there, and paint that old can contain lead. What follows from that is method, not a refusal: sheeting, sealed doorways, dust kept where it is made, and a cleanup Blue Island homeowners should expect to see done properly.

The rule does not say a Blue Island house cannot be painted. It says how the area gets sealed off, how the dust is contained and how the site is left. The trigger in a 1961-median room is about six square feet of disturbed paint, twenty outside, and any window replacement or demolition at all.

None of it is graded at the town line. The rule attaches to a build year and to the work being done, so the number worth checking is the one on your own deed in Blue Island.

The Census publishes a pre-1980 bucket rather than a pre-1978 one, and on that measure 71.9 percent of the housing sits on the older side of the line in Blue Island. Housing that old falls under the federal Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, which covers any work disturbing paint in a home built before 1978. Illinois is not an authorized state for it, so EPA runs it here directly.

Ask about it early. It changes the sequence of a job rather than the price of the paint, and a contractor who has thought about it will tell you in plain terms what happens on day one.
